transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I came in because I can’t stop focusing on this rough, kind of sunken-looking patch on my face. I see it in the mirror and in photos, and it makes one side of my face look old and beat-up to me. Other people say they barely notice anything, but I can’t seem to stop seeing it.

Do you find yourself spending a lot of time thinking about this patch on your face, or do you feel driven to perform any behaviors—like checking mirrors, touching your face, or trying to hide it—to deal with your concerns?

Yeah, I do. Before work I’ll stand in the bathroom and keep checking it, turning my face different ways under the light. I’ll rub at the spot too, like maybe it’ll look smoother or something.

If I’m going somewhere, like my sister’s game night, I’ll do the same thing. Sometimes I pull a hat down low to cover it, and if I think it looks too obvious, I’ll just make up a reason not to go.
When you check the patch on your face or try to cover it up, is it mainly because you feel like it makes your face look ugly or defective in a way that other people don’t seem to notice?

Yes. That’s pretty much it. I look at it and it just seems like this rough, sunken spot that makes my face look messed up, like older and worn out on that side. Other people tell me they barely see it, but I keep seeing it every time I look in the mirror or at a photo.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms of preoccupation with a perceived defect in appearance, repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, touching, camouflaging), and significant distress align specifically with Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.22). Other candidates (F42.2, F32.0) are ruled out due to absence of key features like obsessions with non-defect appearance concerns (F42.2) or depressive episode criteria (F32.0).
